comments.author: Aditi Kulkarni
comments.comment: Our rubric has 4 levels for each answer: correct, partly correct, wrong, and refused. We almost left out 'refused' because we thought it would never happen, but it turned out to be important: Claude refused 3 questions about exam dates and told us to check the official notice instead. comments.author: Riya Kapoor
comments.comment: Interesting finding from our group: Gemini answers in Hindi when the question is asked in Hinglish, but ChatGPT almost always replies in English, even when we asked it in Hinglish three times in a row. For our college this matters, because a lot of first-years are much more comfortable in Hindi, especially for things like fee and hostel rules. We're not sure which behaviour is 'better' though. Should a college bot follow the language of the question, or stick to English because the official documents are in English?

comments.author: Aditi Kulkarni
comments.comment: Sorry to be blunt, but your evaluation table is useless right now. 'Good' and 'bad' are not criteria, they're just feelings. Two people reading the same answer will give it different scores, and then your 70% figure means nothing. Write down what makes an answer good (correct facts, cites the right rule, says 'I don't know' when it should), score each answer against that, and have two people score separately. Then the table will actually be worth reading, and the rest of your report looks solid.

comments.author: Ananya Bose
comments.comment: Our chatbot evaluation is done. The main finding: it is great at explaining concepts, like what a backlog is or how CGPA is calculated, but bad at anything date-related: deadlines, holidays, exam schedules, the last date to pay fees. The worst part is that it never says 'I don't know'. It just gives a confident, specific, wrong date. We think the college should only use a bot like this for general questions, and point students to the official notice board for anything with a date.

comments.author: Devika Nair
comments.comment: We compared answers to 'Is attendance compulsory?' across three bots. All of them said 75% is the minimum, which is the common rule in many colleges, but our college's rule is 80%, and below 65% you're not allowed to sit the exam at all. None of them mentioned that. A student who trusted the bot could genuinely get debarred. Generic answers that sound right are a big risk for a college FAQ bot, so we've made 'college-specific accuracy' our most heavily weighted criterion.

comments.author: Aditi Kulkarni
comments.comment: We had the same problem with 'helpfulness' feeling subjective. What worked for us: two people scored every answer separately without talking, using a short written description of each score. Then we only discussed the answers where we disagreed, which was about 1 in 6. Most disagreements were about answers that were correct but too long. We ended up adding 'gets to the point' as its own criterion, and the disagreements dropped a lot.

comments.author: Siddhant Roy
comments.comment: We asked the bot the same question five times in five separate chats: 'Can I get a refund if I leave the hostel in the middle of the semester?' We got three different answers: a full refund, a partial refund, and no refund. The college rule is a partial refund minus one month. If a student asks once, they have no way of knowing they got the wrong version. So I think consistency, getting the same answer when asked again, should be a rubric item on its own, not part of accuracy.
